newsitem.title: USA: INTERVIEW - Nucor Q2 earnings to beat Q1's.
newsitem.headline: INTERVIEW - Nucor Q2 earnings to beat Q1's.

text.p: Buoyed by lower costs, Nucor Corp's second-quarter earnings should be higher than its first-quarter performance of $0.74 per share, John Correnti, Nucor's president, said Monday.

"We should have a better second quarter," Correnti told Reuters in a brief interview. "We posted $0.74 in the first quarter. A lot of that had to do with start-up costs (at its Berkley, S.C., mill). Berkley is now turning the corner from a start-up situation to a profitable situation."

Nucor's new flat-rolled steel mill in Berkley began production last year and start-up costs have dampened earnings. Correnti said most of those costs are now behind the company and he also expects '98 to be more profitable than this year.
"I expect '98 to be better than '97," he said. "Nucor has a lot of start-up costs behind it now."
Wall Street's consensus estimate for this year is $3.34 per share, based on 14 estimates ranging from $3.00 to $3.75, according to First Call. The consensus estimate for '98 is $3.78.
Nucor, the nation's largest steel minimill producer, posted full-year earnings of $2.83 per share in '96.

Commenting on projections for this year, Correnti said, "What I've said publicly before is that I'm comfortable with $0.70 in the first quarter, $0.80 in the second quarter, $0.90 in the third quarter and $1.00 in the fourth quarter."
The consensus estimates for the remaining three quarters of this year are $0.83, $0.88, and $0.91, respectively.
Separately, Correnti said Nucor may build two or three additional steel plants in the next five to six years to capture up to 20 percent of the total U.S. steel market.

"We're looking at a lot of things," Correnti said. "Nucor has about 11 million tons of (steel) capacity; that's less than 10 percent of the total U.S. market. I wouldn't be uncomfortable having 20 percent of the market.
"That's not going to take place overnight. In the next five to six years we might add two or three more plants."
Correnti declined to comment on whether the plants would produce flat-rolled or structural steel products.
Nucor may also expand capacity at some of its existing plants, he said.

Those projects could include boosting flat-rolled production at its Berkley plant to 2.6 million tons a year from its current capacity of 1.8 million tons and building a new cold-rolling or galvanizing line at its Hickman, Arkansas facility to produce more value-added products.

Nucor has been expanding its existing facilities recently. The company said last month it would begin producing structural products at its Berkley plant, which currently produces only flat-rolled steel.
